chunks: System on module versus SoC. The question: What is a system on module (SoM)? What is the difference/tradeoffs vs a SoC?
A SoC ("What is a system on chip") is a chip.
A system on module (SoM) is a small circuit board that carries a SoC plus memory, storage and power parts, and plugs into your own board. It is a ready-made mini computer.
Using one saves design time and risk. Designing around the bare chip costs more up front but is cheaper per unit when you make many.
Think of a restaurant choosing between a ready-made sauce and cooking it from scratch.
The ready-made sauce lets you open tomorrow and avoids kitchen mistakes, but you pay more per serving.
Cooking from scratch takes time to get right, but costs less per serving once you serve thousands. The module is the ready-made sauce.
One difference: a module is a board, so it adds height and a connector to your product.
The module hides the hardest board-level design (DDR, power sequencing) behind a connector.
The carrier board then needs only the interfaces, which is why it can be a simpler, lower-layer-count PCB.
SoM (system on module): a small board with a SoC, memory, storage and power parts, sold as one unit.
Carrier board: your product's own board, with connectors and sensors, that the module plugs into. Chip-down: placing the bare SoC and its parts directly on your product board.
Board-support package (BSP): the ready-made startup software and drivers (code that runs each part) for one board.
NRE (non-recurring engineering): the one-time cost of designing and getting a design working. Break-even volume: the number of units where two options cost the same in total.
A module design has an NRE of 60,000 USD and costs 38 USD per unit. A chip-down design has an NRE of 250,000 USD and costs 24 USD per unit.
Chip-down costs 190,000 USD more up front but saves 14 USD per unit, so break-even is 190 000 over 14 about 13 600 units.
At 1,000 units, the module averages 98 USD per unit and chip-down 274 USD. That is the whole idea.
"A SoM is a small board containing a SoC plus DRAM, flash and power management, plugged into your carrier board.
The SoC is the silicon; the SoM is a ready-made mini-system around it.
A SoM cuts time to market and layout risk, since DDR routing, sequencing and the software support are done, but costs more per unit and locks you into its form factor.
Chip-down with the bare SoC wins at high volume."
